lessons.title: Introduction and Why It Matters
lessons.body:
In Africa, your ironwork faces harsh sun, heavy rain, dust, and humidity. Without proper weatherproofing, even the best-welded gate will rust within one rainy season. Rust doesn't just look badâit weakens the metal, causing cracks and eventually failure. For a business, a rusty gate means unhappy customers, no referrals, and lost income. This module teaches you how to protect your work so it lasts for years, even in coastal or humid regions.

Weatherproofing has two main parts: surface preparation and coating. First, you must remove all rust, mill scale, and dirt. Then you apply a protective layerâprimer and paint, or galvanizing, or powder coating. In Africa, we often use red oxide primer followed by enamel paint because these are affordable and available in local markets. For high-end jobs, hot-dip galvanizing is best but expensive. Many artisans start with paint and later upgrade.

Why does it matter? A well-finished gate can sell for 30% more than a rusty one. Customers judge your work by its shine and smoothness. Also, proper finishing prevents callbacksâyou won't have to repaint a gate after three months. In dusty areas like the Sahel, a good coat of paint also makes cleaning easier. In coastal cities like Mombasa or Lagos, salt air speeds rust; you need extra coats and rust-resistant primers.

Think of finishing as the final 20% of your job that gives 80% of the impression. A perfect weld means nothing if the gate rusts in six months. So take your time. Prepare the metal properly. Use quality products. And always test your finish on a small piece before applying to the whole project. This module will show you exactly how.

lessons.title: Tools and Materials
lessons.body:
To weatherproof ironwork, you need a few basic tools and materials. For surface prep: a wire brush (hand or drill-mounted), sandpaper (80 to 120 grit), a grinder with a wire cup wheel, and a scraper. A needle gun is great for heavy rust but expensive; most start with a grinder. For cleaning: rags, mineral spirits or acetone, and a clean bucket. For application: paintbrushes (2-inch and 4-inch), rollers for large flat areas, and a spray gun if you can afford one. Spray guns give a smoother finish but need a compressor.

Materials: red oxide primer (oil-based), enamel paint (gloss or semi-gloss), thinner (matching the paint), and optionally a rust converter (like phosphoric acid) for hard-to-remove rust. For galvanizing, you need a galvanizing plantânot practical for small workshops. Instead, use cold galvanizing compound (zinc-rich paint) as a touch-up. For powder coating, you need a powder coating gun and ovenâagain, for advanced setups. In Africa, common brands include Crown, Dulux, and local mixes. Buy from reputable suppliers; cheap paint peels quickly.

Safety gear: gloves (nitrile or leather), safety glasses, dust mask (for sanding), and respirator (for spraying). You also need a well-ventilated area. For outdoor work, a shade cloth to prevent direct sun from drying paint too fast. For mixing, a clean metal or plastic container and a stirring stick. Keep a fire extinguisher nearbyâpaint and thinner are flammable.

For small jobs, a wire brush and sandpaper cost less than $5. A grinder with wire wheel costs $30-$50. A spray gun starts at $20. Primer and paint: a 4-litre tin of red oxide primer costs about $10-$15; enamel paint similar. Thinner: $5 per litre. These are affordable for a beginner. Always buy extraârunning out mid-job causes uneven coats. Store materials in a cool, dry place, away from children.

lessons.title: Step by Step Method
lessons.body:
Step 1: Clean the metal. Remove all dirt, oil, and grease with a rag soaked in mineral spirits. If there's old paint, strip it with a paint remover or sand it off. Step 2: Remove rust. Use a grinder with a wire cup wheel or a wire brush. For tight corners, use sandpaper. Rust must be completely goneâif you see black spots, keep grinding. For light rust, apply a rust converter and let it dry. Step 3: Sand smooth. Use 80-grit sandpaper to smooth welds and rough areas, then 120-grit for a fine finish. Wipe with a tack cloth or a rag dampened with thinner.

Step 4: Apply primer. Stir the red oxide primer thoroughly. Apply a thin, even coat with a brush or spray gun. Don't glob it onâthin coats dry better and adhere stronger. Let it dry according to the can (usually 4-6 hours). If you're in a humid area, wait longer. Step 5: Sand lightly. Once primer is dry, sand lightly with 220-grit sandpaper to remove bumps. Wipe clean. Step 6: Apply topcoat. Use enamel paint. For a glossy finish, apply two thin coats, waiting 24 hours between coats. Use a brush for small areas, roller for flat panels, spray for complex shapes. Always paint in the shadeâdirect sun causes bubbles.

Step 7: Check for missed spots. Look at the gate from different angles. Touch up any bare metal with primer, then paint. Step 8: Let it cure. Full cure takes 7 days. Don't install or handle roughly for at least 48 hours. In rainy season, cover with a tarp if outside. For galvanizing: if you can afford it, take your piece to a galvanizer. They dip it in molten zinc. This gives 20+ years of protection. After galvanizing, you can paint for aestheticsâuse a primer made for galvanized metal (like zinc phosphate).

For small decorative pieces, you can also use powder coating. But that requires a shop. Most beginners start with paint. Remember: preparation is 80% of the job. A poorly prepared surface will peel, no matter how good the paint.

lessons.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
lessons.body:
Mistake 1: Painting over rust. This is the biggest killer. Rust will continue under the paint and push it off. Fix: Always remove rust completely. If you can't, use a rust converter first. Mistake 2: Not cleaning oil or grease. Oil prevents paint from sticking. Fix: Wipe with mineral spirits or acetone before painting. Mistake 3: Applying thick coats. Thick paint skins over but stays wet underneath, causing wrinkles and slow drying. Fix: Apply thin coats, more of them. Mistake 4: Painting in direct sunlight. The surface gets too hot, paint dries too fast, and you get bubbles and brush marks. Fix: Work in shade or on a cloudy day. Mistake 5: Using the wrong primer. For galvanized metal, use a zinc-rich primer. For bare steel, red oxide is fine. For aluminum, use an etch primer. Fix: Match primer to metal.

Mistake 6: Not thinning paint properly. If paint is too thick, it won't flow; too thin, it runs. Fix: Follow the can instructions. Add thinner slowly, stir well. Mistake 7: Skipping the second coat. One coat never covers fully. Fix: Always apply at least two topcoats. Mistake 8: Handling too soon. Paint feels dry but isn't cured. Fix: Wait 48 hours before moving, 7 days for full cure. Mistake 9: Ignoring weather. Humidity above 85% or temperature below 10Â°C stops curing. Fix: Check the forecast. Paint when humidity is below 70% and temp between 15-30Â°C. Mistake 10: Not covering the whole piece. Missed spots rust first. Fix: Use a mirror or light to inspect all sides.

Mistake 11: Using old, clumpy paint. Fix: Strain paint through a fine mesh or cheesecloth. Mistake 12: Not stirring. Pigments settle. Fix: Stir from the bottom up for at least 2 minutes. Mistake 13: Spraying too close or too far. Too close causes runs; too far causes dry spray. Fix: Keep gun 20-25 cm from surface. Mistake 14: Not cleaning the spray gun. Fix: Clean immediately after use with thinner. Mistake 15: Forgetting safety. Fix: Always wear mask and glasses. If you make a mistake, don't panic. Sand it down and redo. Learning from errors makes you a better craftsman.

lessons.title: Safety and Best Practice
lessons.body:
Safety first. Paint and thinner fumes are toxic. Always work in a well-ventilated areaâopen doors and windows, or work outside. If indoors, use a fan to blow fumes away. Wear a respirator (N95 or better) when spraying or sanding. Safety glasses protect your eyes from flying rust and paint. Nitrile gloves protect your skin from solvents. Wear long sleeves and pants to avoid skin contact. Keep a fire extinguisher nearbyâpaint and thinner are flammable. Never smoke or use open flames near painting area.

Best practices: Always prepare a small test piece first. This helps you check color, drying time, and adhesion. Keep your workspace clean. Dust and dirt ruin a wet paint job. Use a tack cloth before painting. Store paint and solvents in a locked cabinet away from children. Dispose of used rags and empty cans properlyâdon't burn them. In Africa, many artisans work in open-air workshops; that's good for ventilation, but beware of dust and sudden rain. Have a tarp ready to cover your work.

For galvanizing, safety is different: the process uses molten zinc at 450Â°C. Only trained professionals should do it. If you send your work to a galvanizer, ensure they are reputable. For powder coating, the oven is hot and the powder can be explosive if inhaled. Leave it to specialists. For cold galvanizing (zinc-rich paint), treat it like regular paint but with extra ventilation.

Best practice for longevity: Apply a maintenance coat every 2-3 years. Inspect for scratches and touch up immediately. In coastal areas, wash your ironwork with fresh water monthly to remove salt. In dusty areas, wipe with a damp cloth. Keep a record of the paint brand and color for future touch-ups. Teach your customers how to care for their ironworkâthis builds trust and repeat business. Finally, always wear your safety gear. Your health is more important than any job.

lessons.title: Practical Exercise
lessons.body:
For this exercise, you will weatherproof a small ornamental pieceâa simple gate or a decorative panel. You will need: a piece of mild steel (approx. 30cm x 30cm), wire brush, sandpaper (80, 120, 220 grit), red oxide primer, enamel paint (your choice of color), paintbrush, thinner, rags, mineral spirits, and safety gear. Work in a shaded, well-ventilated area.

Step 1: Inspect the metal. Look for rust, oil, and weld spatter. Step 2: Clean with mineral spirits. Wipe dry. Step 3: Remove rust with wire brush and sandpaper. Get into all corners. Step 4: Sand the entire surface with 80-grit, then 120-grit, then 220-grit. Wipe with a tack cloth. Step 5: Apply a thin coat of red oxide primer. Let dry 6 hours. Step 6: Lightly sand with 220-grit. Wipe clean. Step 7: Apply first coat of enamel paint. Let dry 24 hours. Step 8: Apply second coat. Let dry 48 hours. Step 9: Inspect for missed spots. Touch up if needed. Step 10: Test adhesion by pressing a piece of tape on the paint and pulling it off. If paint comes off, you need to redo preparation.

Document your work: take before and after photos. Note the products used, drying times, and any issues. This will help you improve. For a more advanced exercise, try a rust converter on a heavily rusted piece. Or try cold galvanizing spray on a small area. Compare the finish and durability. If you have access to a galvanizer, send a small piece and compare with your painted piece. Leave both outside for a month and observe.

After completing, write a short report: What went well? What would you do differently? How much did materials cost? How long did it take? This exercise prepares you for real client work. Remember, a professional finish is what separates a hobbyist from a craftsman. Practice until you can achieve a smooth, even, rust-free finish every time. Then you can confidently charge more for your work.

quiz.q: What is the main reason weatherproofing is important for ornamental ironwork in Africa?
options: A) To make it look shiny
B) To prevent rust and weakening from sun, rain, and humidity
D) To make it easier to weld
quiz.explanation: Weatherproofing protects against rust and environmental damage, which weakens the metal.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a common weatherproofing method mentioned?
options: A) Red oxide primer and enamel paint
quiz.explanation: Gold electroplating is not a typical weatherproofing method for ornamental ironwork.

quiz.q: Why is surface preparation considered 80% of the job?
options: A) Because it takes the most time
B) Because paint won't adhere properly to a dirty or rusty surface
C) Because it requires expensive tools
D) Because it is the easiest step
quiz.explanation: Proper preparation ensures the coating bonds well and lasts.

quiz.q: What is the recommended grit sequence for sanding before painting?
quiz.explanation: Start with coarse (80) to remove imperfections, then finer (120, 220) for smoothness.

quiz.q: Which tool is best for removing heavy rust from tight corners?
options: C) Grinder with wire cup wheel
quiz.explanation: A grinder with a wire cup wheel reaches into corners and removes rust quickly.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a rust converter?
options: A) To convert rust into a paintable surface
C) To add color to rust
D) To prevent rust from forming
quiz.explanation: Rust converters chemically convert rust into a stable, paintable surface.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid painting in direct sunlight?
options: B) Paint dries too fast causing bubbles and brush marks
quiz.explanation: Direct sun heats the metal, causing paint to dry too quickly and form defects.

quiz.q: How many topcoats of enamel paint are recommended for a durable finish?
quiz.explanation: Two thin coats provide better coverage and durability than one thick coat.

quiz.q: What is the minimum curing time before handling a painted piece roughly?
quiz.explanation: Paint should be left for at least 48 hours before rough handling, though full cure takes 7 days.

quiz.q: Which primer is best for galvanized metal?
quiz.explanation: Zinc-rich primer adheres well to galvanized surfaces.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when applying paint?
quiz.explanation: Thick coats dry unevenly, causing wrinkles and slow curing.

quiz.q: How should you store paint and solvents?
options: A) In a hot, sunny place
B) In a cool, dry, locked cabinet
quiz.explanation: Proper storage prevents accidents and keeps materials usable.

quiz.q: What safety gear is essential when spraying paint?
quiz.explanation: A respirator protects from fumes, and safety glasses protect eyes from splatter.

quiz.q: Why is it important to test adhesion with tape?
options: B) To see if paint sticks properly
quiz.explanation: The tape test reveals poor adhesion, indicating preparation problems.

quiz.q: What is the recommended distance for spray gun from surface?
quiz.explanation: 20-25 cm gives an even coat without runs or dry spray.

quiz.q: Which of these is a best practice for maintaining painted ironwork?
options: C) Leave it in direct rain
quiz.explanation: Immediate touch-ups prevent rust from spreading.

quiz.q: What is cold galvanizing?
quiz.explanation: Cold galvanizing uses a zinc-rich paint for touch-up protection.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid using old, clumpy paint?
options: B) It leaves a rough, uneven finish
quiz.explanation: Clumps create an uneven surface and poor adhesion.

quiz.q: What is the first step in the practical exercise?
options: B) Clean the metal with mineral spirits
quiz.explanation: Cleaning removes oil and dirt before any sanding or painting.

quiz.q: How often should you apply a maintenance coat of paint?
quiz.explanation: A maintenance coat every 2-3 years extends the life of the finish.

quiz.q: What is the danger of using a spray gun without cleaning it?
options: B) It clogs and sprays unevenly
quiz.explanation: Dried paint clogs the nozzle, causing sputtering and uneven spray.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a sign of poor preparation?
options: A) Paint peeling after a week
quiz.explanation: A smooth, glossy finish indicates good preparation and application.

quiz.q: What should you do if you miss a spot while painting?
options: B) Touch up with primer then paint
quiz.explanation: Missed spots rust first, so touch up with primer and paint.

quiz.q: Why is ventilation important when painting?
options: B) To avoid inhaling toxic fumes
quiz.explanation: Paint and thinner fumes are harmful; good ventilation keeps you safe.

quiz.q: What is the best way to check if paint is fully cured?
options: A) Touch it with your finger
B) Press a coin on it
quiz.explanation: Full cure takes about 7 days; testing too early can damage the finish.

quiz.q: Which of these is a common mistake when mixing paint?
quiz.explanation: Not stirring leaves pigments settled, causing uneven color and finish.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a tack cloth?
options: B) To remove dust before painting
quiz.explanation: A tack cloth picks up fine dust that can ruin a paint job.

quiz.q: In coastal areas, what extra step helps prevent rust?
options: A) Wash with fresh water monthly
B) Apply one coat of paint
D) Leave it in salt air
quiz.explanation: Fresh water rinses away salt, which accelerates rust.

quiz.q: What is the recommended temperature range for painting?
quiz.explanation: 15-30Â°C is ideal for proper curing and adhesion.

quiz.q: Why should you document your work in the practical exercise?
options: B) To learn from mistakes and improve
quiz.explanation: Documentation helps identify what works and what needs improvement.
